title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Here's today's research digest across your tracked topics — anti-aging, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, integrative/targeted options for HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. Today leans into fresh 2026 trial and meta-analysis data: mTOR-dosing and mitophagy trials, HIIT intensity-zone nuances, a durable pelvic-floor electrical-stimulation RCT, genomic predictors of T-DXd response, and the AASM's combination-therapy guidance. Findings are drawn from PubMed, Nature/Nature Aging, Frontiers, Springer, AASM, and ClinicalTrials.gov — citations are linked as chips below each section. Informational only — discuss anything you'd act on with a clinician.

sections.body:
The longevity field is doubling down on **getting the dose right** for mTOR inhibitors and on **mitophagy inducers** with real human endpoints.

- **Rapamycin/everolimus dosing goes rigorous.** The NIA-backed **RESTOR** trial (*NCT06658093*, UT Health San Antonio; recruiting, started March 2026) is an exploratory PK/PD study in healthy adults ~65–90 designed to find a **dose and schedule that safely lowers mTOR activity to youthful levels** — and it explicitly expects the **optimal dose to differ between women and men**. A separate UT Southwestern RCT (*NCT05237687*) is testing very-low-dose **sirolimus (0.5 mg/day)** against standard care for functional aging biomarkers. Takeaway: the science is still pinning down *safe, effective dosing* — off-label self-experimentation is premature.
- **Urolithin A for immune aging (new human RCT).** A 2025 *Nature Aging* randomized, double-blind trial ("MitoImmune," 50 healthy middle-aged adults, **1,000 mg/day for 28 days**) found that the mitophagy inducer **urolithin A expanded naive-like, less-exhausted CD8+ T cells** (treatment difference 0.50 percentage points; P = 0.04) and **boosted CD8+ fatty-acid-oxidation capacity** (+14.72 pp; P = 0.006) — early evidence it may counter "inflammaging."
- **On the horizon.** An **NIH/NIA** trial of **urolithin A on glucose metabolism** in adults 55+ (*NCT06274749*, 1 g/day for 8 weeks) is slated to begin **recruiting around Aug 25, 2026**.

Practical framing: prefer interventions with human RCTs, expect **modest** effects, and treat single-supplement "longevity" claims with skepticism.

sections.body:
This week's evidence gets **specific about intensity, modality, and pairing** — HIIT reliably improves cardio fitness and trims fat percentage, but the scale often barely moves without added strength work.

- **Intensity zones matter for what you're chasing.** A 2026 *Frontiers in Physiology* meta-analysis (14 RCTs) found HIIT significantly lowered **BMI and body-fat %** but **not total body weight**. Signals in the data: shorter, frequent bouts at **Zone 4 (~80–89% HR-peak)** trended toward BMI reduction, while **longer programs (>12 weeks) at Zone 5 (≥90% HR-peak)** favored body-fat loss. **Running-based** HIIT trended better than cycling (interpret cautiously given small samples).
- **HIIT vs. steady-state.** A 2026 *BMC Sports Science* meta-analysis (19 RCTs) reported HIIT **outperformed moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) for VO2peak** in sedentary and obese groups and reduced BMI more in obese populations, with **cycling HIIT comparable to MICT** for overall body composition — good news if you prefer the bike.
- **Postmenopausal women.** A 12-week RCT (*NCT07302191*, 45 women with overweight/obesity, 3×/week) found both **HIIT and concurrent (HIIT + resistance) training** cut body weight, BMI, abdominal fat, triglycerides, LDL, glucose, and insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) vs. controls — with **concurrent training slightly ahead on body composition.**

Bottom line: intensity drives the cardio and metabolic wins; **add resistance training**, progress volume gradually, and keep recovery adequate.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** remains the evidence-based **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). New 2026 data clarify **which add-ons pay off** — especially for women whose muscles are too weak for training alone to work well.

- **Adding stimulation when muscles are very weak (durable benefit).** A 2026 multicentre, double-blind RCT (*Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol*, 42 women with SUI and very weak pelvic floors) added **sEMG-triggered intravaginal electrical stimulation** to supervised PFMT (3×/week for 10 weeks + daily home program). The stimulation group gained **more pelvic-floor strength that lasted to 12 months** (+0.59 Oxford points; P = 0.009) and, at one year, had **fewer weekly leaks (−1.51 episodes), less pad use (−2.6 pads/day), and better ICIQ-SF scores (−5.20)**. Meaningful patient-rated improvement: **65% vs. 18%** of controls.
- **What ranks best overall.** A 2026 *Frontiers in Medicine* network meta-analysis (49 RCTs, 5,432 women, postpartum SUI) ranked **PFMT + vaginal weights** highest for reducing **objective leakage** (pad test), while **PFMT + biofeedback + electrical stimulation** and **aerobic exercise** led for **quality of life**, and **PFMT + vaginal weights or biofeedback/e-stim** led for **muscle strength**.

Key point: **correct technique and consistency beat sheer reps.** Confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback; supervised programs generally outperform unsupervised ones, and targeted add-ons help most when baseline strength is low.

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
For HER2-positive disease that also carries **TP53/p53 alterations**, "alternative" is best read as **evidence-based, biomarker-guided strategy alongside standard care** — not a replacement for it.

- **Genomics is starting to predict who benefits from T-DXd.** An **AACR 2026** analysis (Tempus real-world + genomic data across HER2 subtypes) found **TP53 was the most commonly mutated gene (48%)**. Notably, **PIK3CA mutations tracked with better response** to fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) in HER2+ disease (improved response, progression-free and overall survival signals), while **DYNC2H1 mutations tracked with worse outcomes**, especially in HER2-low tumors — early support for **using tumor genomics to personalize T-DXd**.
- **Why HER2;p53 co-mutant tumors are a special case.** A key mechanistic study (*PubMed/PMC*, 2025) showed these co-mutant tumors are **resistant to neratinib alone** but stay **sensitive to the topoisomerase-I (TOP1) payload** carried by T-DXd — because mutant-p53 tumors show increased histone acetylation, open chromatin, and hyper-transcription of DNA-repair genes. **Neratinib + T-DXd** was highly effective preclinically and is being tested in a **phase 1 trial (NCI ETCTN 10495, NCT05372614)**.
- **Integrative add-ons.** Evidence-based supportive measures (e.g., correcting vitamin D deficiency, an anti-inflammatory dietary pattern) may complement treatment, but **supplements can interact with targeted therapy** — coordinate anything you add with your oncology team.

Important framing: much of this is **early or investigational** evidence. Use integrative and biomarker-guided options as *informed additions* discussed with an oncologist — not substitutes for HER2-targeted therapy. Note that **germline TP53** alterations (Li-Fraumeni) also carry genetic-counseling implications.

sections.body:
For chronic, restless, or disjointed sleep, 2026 guidance keeps **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements**.

- **CBT-I first, medication selectively.** The AASM's 2026 clinical practice guideline on *combination* therapy (with a companion systematic review and GRADE assessment) issued two conditional recommendations: **CBT-I + medication beats medication alone**, but combination is **not** better than **CBT-I alone** — because CBT-I tends to deliver **durable** improvement without drug risks. In the underlying meta-analysis, **no single drug or drug class emerged as a preferred add-on**, and benefits of adding medication were small and outcome-specific (mostly modest gains in total sleep time).
- **Where medications fit.** European guideline evidence supports **dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs)** — e.g., daridorexant, lemborexant, suvorexant — for **up to ~3 months**, and **prolonged-release melatonin** as an option **for adults ~55+** (short-to-medium term). **Immediate-release melatonin and ramelteon are generally not recommended** for chronic insomnia *except* when a **circadian** problem (jet lag, shift work) is driving symptoms.
- **A note on habits.** Guidelines specifically caution that **sleep hygiene advice alone is not an effective standalone treatment** — it's a supporting layer, not the therapy.

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If disrupted sleep persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I** (in-person or digital).
